title: Check a small engine's oil with the dipstick: pull, wipe, reseat, read the level, mark it on the check card, and reseat
instruction: Check the oil level on the engine with the dipstick, mark it on the check card with the puck, then put everything back.
context: Checking the oil with the dipstick is a core duty of automotive service technicians and mechanics (BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook, SOC 49-3023, about 826,000 jobs) on every oil service and inspection, and of small engine mechanics on mowers and generators (SOC 49-3053). The first pull is never read: oil splashed up the fill tube coats the blade above the true level. So the dipstick is pulled, wiped on a rag, pushed back in until the cap seats, pulled again and held still, tip down, to read the level, and pushed back in until it seats so dirt cannot get into the crankcase. The level found (ADD, OK or OVER) goes on the inspection checklist, because it decides the next job: add oil, or drain an overfill. A first-pull reading overstates the oil and can hide a low level.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A bench model of a small four-stroke engine, as on a lawn mower or portable generator, is fixed on the table: a wooden mounting board (x 22 to 38, y -22 to -7, 0.8 cm thick), an aluminum crankcase and cylinder block (x 27 to 37, y -21 to -9, up to z 7) under a red flywheel shroud (to z 10), and a fill boss on the crankcase's front. A yellow oil fill tube, 2.4 cm across with a 2.0 cm bore, rises from the boss to its mouth at z 8.5, on an axis at x 25, y -12. The dipstick sits seated in the tube: a steel blade 1.0 x 0.3 x 8 cm with black ADD and FULL marks 0.8 and 2.0 cm from the tip and a crosshatch between them, a yellow cap disc 3.2 cm across and 1 cm tall resting on the tube's rim, and a yellow T-handle 3.5 cm wide (along y), 1.8 cm thick and 3.5 cm tall on top; 12.5 cm overall, 40 g. It slides only along the tube's axis and falls back down the tube if let go. The blade's lower 6 cm carries an amber smear of oil (drawn), the false first reading. The true level changes from trial to trial and shows on the blade only after a wipe and a full reseat: 0.4 cm from the tip (below ADD), 1.4 cm (between the marks) or 2.7 cm (above FULL), each 4 mm or more from a mark. A folded blue shop rag, a pad 4 x 4 x 2.5 cm of 40 g, lies loose on the table centered at x 26, y 10. An oil check card, a dark gray tray 6 x 16 x 1 cm, is fixed to the table centered at x 35, y 10. It has three pockets 4.4 cm square and 5 mm deep, centered at y 15.2 (ADD), y 10 (OK) and y 4.8 (OVER). Each pocket is labelled on its floor with a white symbol 2.8 cm long in 6 mm strokes, so it reads without color: ADD is an amber floor with a minus sign, OK a green floor with a check mark, OVER a red floor with a plus sign. A white marker puck, 3 cm across, 2 cm tall and 15 g, stands loose on the table at x 20, y 15. Both arms start at their home poses.
scoring: q is the dipstick cap's height above its seat. Out means q of at least the blade length plus 5 mm, so the tip is clear of the mouth and the blade can be wiped and read. Seated means q of 3 mm or less: a cap lifted more than 3 mm leaves the blade short of the oil and lets dirt in, and a real trial checks the gap under the cap with a 3 mm feeler strip. Held means both fingers of a gripper touching the T-handle with their opening stopped by it (across its 1.8 cm thickness or 3.5 cm width); an empty fist, an open hand or one finger does not count, and the video shows the grip. Wipe: the first pull's blade is smeared above the true level, so it must be wiped before the reading means anything. The rag touches the blade when its middle is within 2.7 cm of the blade's axis (half the 4 cm pad, the blade's half-thickness and 0.5 cm of cloth pressed round it), its outline is within 2 mm of the blade's faces (so a rigid pad held clear does not count), and its height overlaps the blade above the mouth. The blade is wiped once the rag's middle has slid, while touching, over 80% (3.2 cm) of the blade's lower 4 cm in that pull. Slides count only between two touching steps and at most 5 mm a step, so dabs and jumps add nothing. The 80% leaves 8 mm of slack for the arm's lag. Two strokes in one pull add up, the tip going back into the tube clears the count, and either hand may move. A real trial checks in the video that the rag is drawn along at least 3.2 cm of the lower blade and that the blade comes away clean. Reseat: the wiped blade pushed in by hand until seated, because the second pull reads true only from a full seat. A part-way push that comes out again smears the blade again, and a drop or a seat without a wipe restarts the procedure. Reading: after the reseat, the dipstick pulled out again and held out and still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s, long enough to look at a still blade; the video's timer measures it. The oil level is set per trial below ADD, between the marks or above FULL, and shows on the blade only after the wipe and reseat. Report: the robot cannot speak, so it marks the level it read by leaving the puck in the ADD, OK or OVER pocket of the check card, as a mechanic ticks the inspection checklist. The puck is in a pocket when its middle is within 1.2 cm of the pocket's middle (a puck lying flat in the 4.4 cm pocket is at most 7 mm off) and its bottom is 2 mm or more below the card's top (down in the 5 mm pocket, not on a rim or a wall). It counts at the end, at rest and let go (no gripper's palm or fingers within 2 mm of it, the solver's resting gap), because a puck still in the hand has not marked anything. A top photo shows the pocket and a side look shows it is down in it. A puck in any pocket for 2 steps (0.1 s) before the reading is a guess, since the level was not yet known; the video shows when it goes in. Scores: doing nothing scores 0. A wrong report or a guess scores 0, whatever else was done, because a wrong level on the checklist sends the next job the wrong way (oil added to a full engine or a low one left running) and a wrong report must never pay more than no report. Also 0 if the blade was never wiped and pushed back in until the cap seats: without that no true reading is possible. 0.25: wiped and seated by hand but no true reading; the procedure that makes a true reading possible is done, the reading is not. 0.5: true reading, no report (puck not in a pocket, on a wall or still held); the level was looked at but not recorded. 0.75: the right report, but the dipstick not seated by hand and let go (no gripper touching the cap or handle), so the engine is left open to dirt, or the rag not put down (at rest, its bottom 1 cm or less above the table, and no gripper touching it), which the instruction asks for. 1.0: all of it. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Always guessing one pocket averages about 0.33 over the three levels, below the 0.5 for reading without reporting, so guessing never pays.
reset_notes: Seat the dipstick and put the rag back at x 26, y 10 and the puck at x 20, y 15. For a real trial, roll a die for the level (1-2 below ADD, 3-4 between the marks, 5-6 above FULL), set it with a syringe of oil, and smear oil on the blade's lower 6 cm and up the inside of the tube. In the sim the seeded reset picks the level (OIL_CASE=low, ok or over sets it); with no jitter it is between the marks.
fidelity: The dipstick is real size for a mower or generator engine. It stays on the tube's axis when out (a guide), so the sim skips lining the tip up with the 2.0 cm bore; a real trial with a free dipstick tests that, with about 5 mm of play. The oil film, its wiping and the trial's level are drawn from the scorer's state; a real trial uses real oil, seen on the blade. The rag is a rigid pad. The demo is scripted and told the level; the scored policy must read the band off the blade.
